power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: While bipolar disorder has a positive genetic correlation (r~0.3) with educational attainment (EA), individuals with bipolar disorder diagnoses have lower EA in adulthood.

To clarify this paradox, we hypothesise that bipolar disorder and educational outcomes share a positive genetic association, reflected in high academic performance earlier in life, but that emerging bipolar disorder symptoms disrupt academic trajectories, leading to the observed poor long-term educational outcomes.
Methods.
We employed a sibling comparison design across four population-based cohorts (Ntotal = 1,145,795 siblings).

First, we tested the association between bipolar disorder polygenic scores (PGS) and educational outcomes (EA and academic performance) in the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and UK Biobank (UKB).

Second, we examined associations between academic performance at ages 10, 12, 13, and 14 and subsequent bipolar disorder diagnosis using registry data from Statistics Netherlands and Statistics Norway (with the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements Databases).
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Findings.

Siblings with higher bipolar disorder PGS had significantly higher EA (βW = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.05], N=16,746) as well as higher academic performance at age 10 (0.03 [0.01, 0.05], N=17,677) in MoBa.

Secondly, individuals with bipolar disorder had better overall academic performance than their unaffected sibling at ages 10 (HRW = 1.12 [1.02, 1.22], N=343,898) and 12 (1.59 [1.16, 2.19], N=619,796).
However, individuals with bipolar disorder experienced a decline in academic performance at ages 13 (0.84 [0.73, 0.96], N=320,342) and 14 (0.72 [0.61, 0.85], N=299,039).
Interpretation.
Bipolar disorder shares a positive genetic association with educational outcomes, reflected in early academic advantage.
This is followed by an academic decline in mid-adolescence, highlighting the period of educational disruption associated with bipolar disorder.

Bipolar disorder is associated with significant psychosocial, occupational and socioeconomic disability. [1] [2] [3] This burden extends to educational settings, as evidenced by high levels of school dropout, 4 lower likelihood of completing a university degree, 5 and ultimately, lower educational attainment (EA) compared to the general population. 6 Paradoxically, the rise of behavioural genetics research has consistently demonstrated a positive genetic association between bipolar disorder and educational outcomes, implying a shared genetic liability. [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] For example, EA is shown to be positively associated with bipolar disorder polygenic scores (PGS). 12- 15 A PGS is a single value estimate of an individual's probabilistic genetic risk for a phenotype, calculated as a sum of genetic variants, weighted by their corresponding effect sizes derived from summary statistic data. 16 These findings imply that on average, individuals with a higher probabilistic genetic risk for bipolar disorder are predicted to have better educational outcomes.

text.text: Deviations to the preregistration are outlined in Supplementary Methods 2.

We used two complementary analyses, first testing the association between bipolar disorder PGS and educational outcomes (EA and academic performance), and secondly the association between academic performance and subsequent bipolar disorder diagnosis.
We employed a sibling comparison design, which assumes that siblings are matched for many familial and socioeconomic factors, as well as ~50% of their DNA.

This facilitates a natural experiment using observational data wherein siblings form a well-matched case-control study. 29, 30 The sibling comparison regression model consists of two components; the between-sibship estimate, which captures differences across families and the withinsibship estimate, which captures associations independent of between-family confounding.

text.text: We also performed all analyses using population-based regressions to contrast against the within-sibship estimates.
Data cleaning procedures for each cohort are outlined in Supplementary Methods 3.

I. The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa): MoBa is a population-based pregnancy cohort, which includes approximately 114,500 children, 95,200 mothers, and 75,200 fathers recruited between 1999 and 2008.
Women consented to participation in 41% of the pregnancies.

Questionnaire data and blood samples were obtained from parents and children during pregnancy and at birth. 31, 32 The pipeline used for quality-control, phasing, and imputation of genotype data in MoBa is described elsewhere. 33, 34 .

text.text: II.

UK Biobank (UKB): UKB is a large-scale prospective cohort study with extensive phenotype and genotype data collected from about 500,000 individuals in the UK, aged between 40 and 69 at the time of recruitment.

Participants were recruited across diverse socioeconomic and ethnic backgrounds as well as a balance of urban and rural settings. 35, 36 Genotype data quality control procedures for UKB are describe elsewhere and in Supplementary Methods 4. 36  In UKB and MoBa, bipolar disorder PGS were constructed using LDPred2-auto, 37 a Bayesian model that estimates the SNP effect sizes from GWAS summary statistics while accounting for linkage . disequilibrium, using assumptions about the trait's polygenicity and SNP heritability (Supplementary Methods 5).

text.text: The highest educational qualification was indexed using The Norwegian Standard Classification of Education (NUS2000) codes in MoBa and the variable 'Qualifications' (UKB ID: 6138) in UKB.

The Norwegian and UKB educational codes were first transformed into the corresponding International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED 2011) codes and subsequently converted into years of education (Supplementary Methods 5).
We included individuals who were 30 years old or older at the time of measurement, to allow sufficient time to attain their maximum EA.
From SSB, we obtained national test scores for mathematics and reading comprehension (in Norwegian) at ages 10, 13, and 14 and for English at ages 10 and 13.
Additionally, we calculated a total score as the mean of mathematics and reading comprehension, excluding English to ensure comparability across years.
In CBS, we extracted national test scores for mathematics, reading comprehension (in Dutch), language (Dutch), and total score measured at age 12.
In SSB, individuals were considered as cases if they had at least five recorded diagnoses for bipolar disorder from any primary or specialized healthcare institutions.
This threshold was established to exclude those with provisional or transient diagnoses.
In CBS, diagnostic information was derived from only specialized mental health care services, and so individuals with just one registered diagnosis were considered as a case.
In both cohorts, those without a diagnosis were considered as controls.
We selected individuals who were at least 15 years old by the final year of available diagnostic data, which was 2025 in SSB and 2016 in CBS.

Across all models, we account for familial clustering by adjusting standard errors using cluster-robust variance estimators using the R packages sandwich and lmtest. 40, 41 Sex, birth year, and birth order were added as covariates in all analyses.

I. Analysis 1: Genetic association of bipolar disorder PGS and educational outcomes Using two separate models, we modelled educational outcomes (EA and academic performance) as the outcome and bipolar disorder PGS as the predictor based on preregistered simulations which indicated greater statistical power compared to the alternative of using EA PGS to predict bipolar disorder diagnosis (Supplementary Methods 6).

We regressed the educational outcome of each sibling on the mean value of the family's bipolar disorder PGS (between-sibship effect) and the deviation of the sibling's bipolar disorder PGS from their family mean (within-sibship effect).
The formula for the sibling comparison regression model was as follows.

Yij = β0 + βB (mXj) + βW (Xij -mXj) + β2 Sexij + β3 BirthYearij + β4 BirthOrderij + ε Where Yij = EA of individual i in family j, βB = between-sibship effect, mXj = mean value of the bipolar disorder PGS for the family j, βW = within-sibship effect, Xij = bipolar disorder PGS of individual i in family j For this model, the hypothesised positive association between bipolar disorder PGS and long-term EA may be attenuated among individuals who develop the disorder, as illness onset can disrupt educational trajectories.
Therefore, we also ran the main EA model with bipolar disorder diagnosis included as a covariate, to examine whether the association changed after correcting for diagnostic status.
II.

Analysis 2: Phenotypic association of academic performance and bipolar disorder diagnosis Cox proportional hazards regression was used to account for those who remained undiagnosed by the end of the observation period.
Undiagnosed individuals were right-censored using the age at their last . available diagnostic record (2025 in SSB and 2016 in CBS).

The formula for the sibling comparison regression model using Cox proportional hazards regression was as follows. hij(t) = h0(t) exp [βB mXj + βW(Xij -mXj) + β2 Sexij + β3 Birthyearij + β4 Birthorderij] where hij(t) = hazard of bipolar disorder diagnosis at time t for individual i in family j, h0(t) = unspecified baseline hazard, βB = between-family effect, mXj = mean value of educational achievement of family j, βW = within-sibship effect, Xij = educational achievement of individual i in family j
As an exploratory analysis, we ran the models for ages 13 and 14 with scores from previous ages included in the regression model as covariates.
This adjusted model specifies how the relative change in academic performance across ages is related to bipolar disorder diagnosis, above and beyond an individual's previous academic performance.

Similarly, using test scores from the Netherlands (CBS) at age 12, higher total score was associated with a significantly higher hazard of bipolar disorder diagnosis (HRW = 1.59, 95% CI [1.16, 2.19]).
This positive association was found across all individual test scores namely mathematics, reading comprehension, and language.
At age 13, this positive association was no longer observed in SSB, as the HR was not found to be significantly different than 1.

At age 14, the associations remained null and even turned negative for mathematics scores; the sibling with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder performed worse than their unaffected sibling at age 14, as indicated by the HR value lower than 1 (HRW = 0.90, 95% CI [0.83, 0.98]).

text.text: Correcting for the scores from age 10, the association in age 13 turned negative such that the sibling with bipolar disorder performed worse compared to their unaffected sibling (HRW = 0.84, 95% CI [0.73, 0.96]), corresponding to a 19% higher hazards of diagnosis for a unit-SD decline in academic performance (calculated as ((1/HR) -1 * 100) for HR less than 1).
This trend was also observed for mathematics scores (HRW = 0.88, 95% CI [0.78, 0.99]).

Correcting for scores from age 10 and 13, the association between the decline in academic performance and bipolar disorder diagnosis became even stronger at age 14 (HRW = 0.72, 95% CI [0.61, 0.85]), corresponding to a 38% higher hazard of diagnosis per unit-SD decline in test score.
This was also reflected in mathematics (HRW = 0.78, 95% CI [0.67, 0.90]) as well as reading scores (HRW = 0.86, 95% CI [0.75, 0.98]).

Given that our primary analyses assumed linear associations, we next tested whether the relationship between academic performance and bipolar disorder diagnosis deviated from linearity; we found no strong evidence of non-linearity, except for mathematics and English scores at age 10, for which the spline model had a significant better fit than a linear model (Supplementary Results 8).
Next, we considered whether the wide confidence intervals observed in our CBS estimates reflected low statistical power due to the small number of bipolar disorder cases in this sample.

To address this, we repeated our analyses using the extended dataset available through 2021, which offered a larger number of cases but less precise case ascertainment as it doesn't distinguish between bipolar disorder diagnoses from other substanceinduced mood disorders.
This yielded population-level estimates similar to the primary analysis in direction and magnitude across all tests, but the within-family associations were not significant (Supplementary Results 9).
In the current study, we used a sibling comparison design across four cohorts to examine the complex association between bipolar disorder and educational outcomes.

We found that higher probabilistic genetic risk for bipolar disorder, indexed using PGS, was associated with higher EA, as well as higher early-life academic performance at age 10 but not at ages 13 and 14.

Moreover, using observed academic performance and diagnostic data, we found that individuals with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder academically outperformed their unaffected sibling . at ages 10 and 12.
However, this academic advantage diminished by ages 13 and 14, with a decline in academic performance significantly related to bipolar disorder.

Our findings are consistent with the suggested model which posits that bipolar disorder and educational outcomes share a positive genetic association, reflected in early academic benefit, but that the emergence of bipolar disorder symptoms disrupts educational trajectories, ultimately resulting in poor long-term educational outcomes.

Taken together, we discuss how our research can help explain conflicting findings in literature, provide epidemiological and clinically-relevant insights as well as highlight potential avenues for future research.

text.text: While we found significant positive associations at age 10, they were no longer significant at ages 13 and 14, suggesting that genetic associations are not consistent across development.

This may reflect exogenous influences on education emerging in early adolescence, such as the transition from primary to lower secondary school in Norway at age 13, bringing about changes in schooling environment and peer groups. 44 The divergence with EA also implies that academic performance and EA are not equivalent constructs; national test scores resemble cognitive tests and are less influenced by socioeconomic influences. 45 Our phenotypic investigation of academic performance across ages 10 to 14 revealed that those with bipolar disorder perform well in school at ages 10 and 12 compared to their unaffected siblings, indicated by a 11 to 59% higher hazard of receiving a diagnosis per unit-SD increase in test score.

text.text: This academic advantage attenuated by ages 13 and 14, with the associations no longer significant.

Extending this longitudinal analysis to an adjusted model, we controlled for the influence of previous test scores to reveal that a decrease in academic performance at ages 13 and 14 is associated with bipolar disorder diagnosis; a unit-SD decline in performance at age 13 was associated with 8 -19% increased hazard of getting a diagnosis, and a decline at age 14 was associated with 17 -39% increased hazard.

The emergence of signs of bipolar disorder at such an early age is consistent with previous evidence of a prolonged prodromal period, such as depressive symptoms emerging in mid-adolescence, several years before the first (hypo)manic episode and diagnosis. 47, 48 Additionally, our findings suggest that relative changes in functional performance may be a better marker of psychopathology risk than absolute academic standing, highlighting the importance of longitudinal data in research as well as continuous observations in clinical practice to get a comprehensive understanding of psychiatric epidemiology.

text.text: Moreover, our analyses revealed age-specific effects of bipolar disorder on academic performance across the developmental trajectory, whereas previous studies with conflicting findings examine academic performance measured at a single age, which limits insight into the academic progression of those with bipolar disorder within each cohort. text.text: Second, while the sibling design accounts for unmeasured confounding factors shared by siblings, it does not control for non-shared confounding and measurement error, which has been shown to affect within-sibship estimates. 54 Measurement error in the exposure attenuates within-sibship estimates more than population estimates, particularly when siblings' exposure values are correlated, relevant for our PGS analyses. 55.

text.text: Thirdly, the period of follow-up for bipolar disorder diagnosis was limited to approximately age 30 in SSB and age 24 in CBS.
To address this limitation, we employed a Cox proportional hazards model to account for individuals who remain undiagnosed by the end of the observation period.

But other issues like cross-cohort discrepancies in case definitions, misdiagnosis and undetected illness remain, potentially attenuating the associations studied. 56 Finally, while we know from previous literature and the current study that high academic performance is a key feature of bipolar disorder, 20, 57 it remains unclear whether the decline is specific to bipolar disorder.

text.text: This warrants comparison with longitudinal academic trajectories of those with other severe mental health issues.

In addition, our findings do not provide insight into the specific processes associated with the academic decline in mid-adolescence, and may be related to depressive symptoms, non-specific mental health difficulties, cognitive decline, or other non-cognitive factors. 45, 58, 59 Investigation into these specific vulnerabilities underlying the educational disruption can provide measurable indicators of emerging bipolar disorder with substantial clinical and interventional potential.

text.text: Using two complementary genetically-informed approaches across multiple large-scale cohorts and national registry datasets, we find evidence of a positive genetic association between bipolar disorder and educational outcomes.
Individuals with bipolar disorder outperformed their unaffected sibling in academic performance at ages 10 and 12.
